sentences.text: The skull of the main specimen measured exactly 189 millimeters, which is smaller than the 272-millimeter skull of the larger Zanabazar.
It possessed a long, low head with a depressed snout, sharp teeth, and a relatively large brain.
Fossils were found on July 9, 1923, by a Chinese employee of the American Museum of Natural History expedition named Chih.
The genus was named by paleontologist Osborn in 1924, though he initially intended the name "Ornithoides" before publishing it without a formal description.
The holotype is specimen AMNH 6516, which serves as the primary reference for the species.
Another specimen from the Late Cretaceous of Mongolia was described in 1964, marking the first collection by a professional Mongolian paleontologist.
A juvenile specimen of S. mongoliensis was described in 1993.
Baron Franz Nopcsa coined the name Saurornithoides sauvagei in 1928, but this resulted from a printing error intended for Teinurosaurus sauvagei.
Saurornithoides were predators capable of running fast on their hind legs with excellent sight and hearing.
Saurornithoides likely scoured the Gobi Desert for small mammals or reptiles to eat.
Likely fast and intelligent, it probably roamed the Gobi Desert hunting small mammals and reptiles.
The highly ossified hindlimb of juvenile Saurornithoides suggests they were well developed at birth and required little to no parental care.
Highly ossified hind limbs suggested that Saurornithoides and other troodontids were well-developed at birth and likely required little or no parental care.
Osborn initially classified Saurornithoides in the Megalosauridae due to its resemblance to Velociraptor.
In 1974, Barsbold recognized the connection between Saurornithoides and American forms like Stenonychosaurus and named the family Saurornithoididae.
In 1987, Philip John Currie showed that Saurornithoididae was a junior synonym of Troodontidae, confirming Saurornithoides as a troodontid.
Saurornithoides belongs to the family Troodontidae.
In 2000, Olshevsky renamed Troodon isfarensis Nessov 1995 to Saurornithoides isfarensis.
In 1987, Philip John Currie demonstrated that the concept was a modern synonym of Troodontidae, implying Saurornithoides was also a troodontid.
Its family is Troodontidae.
Saurornithoides lived during the Late Cretaceous period.
Saurornithoides lived during the Late Cretaceous, approximately 75 million years ago in the Campanian stage, in what is now Asia.
It lived from the Cenomanian to the Maastrichtian, between 100.5 and 66 million years ago.
A 2009 study reassigned Saurornithoides junior to its own genus, Zanabazar, due to the description of many more troodontids with cranial material.
A 2009 review found support for linking S. junior to S. mongoliensis to be erroneous, reclassifying it as Zanabazar junior while keeping the species name.
Due to its origin in the Cenomanian of Uzbekistan, it is generally viewed as a different taxon from Saurornithoides.
